title: Continue after a setback
summary: Turn an event into useful information, without judgment.

perspective.title: Move beyond “everything is ruined”
perspective.paragraph1: Here, a “lapse” means an event that does not match the goal you chose. It does not erase the pauses, choices, and observations you have already made.
perspective.paragraph2: In a smoking-cessation study, most reactions grouped under the abstinence violation effect did not predict relapse. Feeling like giving up after the lapse, however, was associated with faster progression to a second lapse.
perspective.paragraph3: Participants who tried a restorative response after the lapse were less likely to have another one that same day. Because the study concerned smoking, this is a useful lead rather than a rule for your situation.
perspective.keyPoint1: A lapse and a lasting return are two different things.
perspective.keyPoint2: A restorative response may help you pick up the thread.
perspective.keyPoint3: Resume the current plan rather than restarting from zero.

compassion.title: Self-compassion is not indulgence
compassion.paragraph1: Many people fear that going easy on themselves amounts to giving up. Experiments suggest the opposite: after a failure, a kind stance toward oneself was associated with more effort to improve.
compassion.paragraph2: One structured self-compassion training program has also shown effects on well-being in a controlled trial, run on a small, mostly female sample. Self-compassion is therefore something you practice as a skill rather than a fixed personality trait.
compassion.paragraph3: One simple formulation: speak to yourself the way you would speak to someone you respect who has just been through the same thing.

adjust.title: Adjust rather than punish
adjust.paragraph1: Look at what came before: time, tiredness, emotion, device, or general context.
adjust.paragraph2: Then choose one limited adjustment. Punishment or an unrealistic goal rarely provides useful information.
adjust.paragraph3: A lapse is also data: it points to a spot in the plan that was not yet covered. That is unpleasant, but it is usable.
adjust.keyPoint1: Look for the situation, not the culprit.
adjust.keyPoint3: Tightening the goal after a lapse rarely makes it more sustainable.

plan.title: A skill, not a fate
plan.paragraph1: Relapse-prevention approaches consider the possibility of a lapse and suggest preparing your response in advance rather than relying only on the hope that it will not happen.
plan.paragraph2: Reviews of these programs show broadly favorable effects on addictive behaviors, with results varying across substances and protocols.
plan.paragraph3: You can prepare three lines: what I do after the lapse, who I can message, and what I look at in my plan before concluding anything.

help.title: Know when to ask for help
help.paragraph1: If loss of control persists, causes severe distress, or has significant consequences, talking to a qualified professional may help.
help.paragraph2: Recent reviews focus mainly on cognitive-behavioral psychotherapies and acceptance-based approaches. They report encouraging results, but study quality is often low and risk of bias high, so effectiveness cannot yet be stated with certainty.
help.paragraph3: Asking for help can be part of the plan; it does not take away from progress already made.

reflectionPrompt: What useful information can you take from the last event without judging yourself?
